You are analyzing an SF1000 TPC-H profiling campaign of StarRocks-on-Sirius (a GPU SQL engine embedded in a StarRocks compute node, "CN").
Read /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/WORKFLOW-PLAN.md first: it lists every evidence file, the tools and the facts already established. Evidence root: /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000. Source tree: /home/prestouser/aocsa/sirius-stacks-wt/perf
(engine C++ under src/, CN Rust under experimental/starrocks/src, translator under experimental/starrocks/crates/starrocks-plan-translator, StarRocks FE Java under experimental/starrocks/starrocks/fe).
Key pre-digested files: /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/results.md (timings per arm), /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/survey/plan-summary.txt and /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/survey/explain/qNN.costs.txt (FE plans), /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/card-compare-cn1.txt and card-compare-cn4.txt (FE estimate vs actual rows per exchange),
/tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/cn1-cnlog.txt / cn4-cnlog.txt (+ .json: per run fragments, declared cardinalities, nixl transmits, OOM reschedules), /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/cn1-quent.txt / cn4-quent.txt / standalone-quent.txt (+ .json: task state time, reservation vs peak, batches, dwell, staging leases),
/tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/cn1-ops.txt etc (per-operator Computing time), /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/standalone/runs/qNN.explain.txt (DuckDB/Sirius plan of the same SQL), /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/cn1/dump/ (FE fragment params + Substrait per fragment), /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/compare-*.txt (oracle correctness).
You may run the python tools in /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000 and read the source; do not modify the source tree, do not start clusters or GPU jobs (they are exclusive resources owned by the orchestrator), do not write outside /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/agent-notes/.
The three focus dimensions are: (A) query planning, (B) cardinality estimation, (C) backpressure (memory pressure, parked intermediates, staging leases, queue waits, OOM reschedules, scaling 1->4 CN).
Every finding must cite concrete evidence (file + the line or number) and, where it proposes a change, name the file/function and rate confidence. Distinguish measured facts from inference.

Your family: broadcast-joins. Queries: q03 q10 q12 q14 q19. Focus: FE BROADCAST of orders/lineitem-sized build sides chosen with cardinality 1; actual rows per exchange; parked bytes and dwell; what DuckDB standalone chose instead (build side, join order).
Work through the evidence for these queries in all arms (cn1, cn4, standalone, plus standalone-failed / q15 canon arms if present), read the relevant source when a mechanism matters (engine.rs run_fragment_inner, local_exchange.rs, gpu_pipeline_executor.cpp reschedule loop, exchange_staging_arena.cpp, the FE StatisticsCalculator and the join distribution rules), and produce 3-8 findings ranked by impact. Prefer fewer, well-evidenced findings. Write your working notes to /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/agent-notes/broadcast-joins.md (tables you computed, commands you ran) and return the findings as structured output.

- ooc-sort-dev: Use when developing, building, testing, or iterating on the disk-backed (out-of-core) sort implementation for cudf-polars in ~/bzaitlen/test-data/ooc-sort/. Covers installing into the rapidsmpf container env, running streaming sort tests, and the phase-by-phase implementation workflow.
- build-errors: Use this skill when the build fails, compilation errors occur, or you see undefined references, linker errors, CUDA compilation issues, missing headers, or template instantiation failures. Analyzes errors, suggests fixes, and iteratively rebuilds until success.
- build-sirius-starrocks: Build the Sirius-as-StarRocks-CN stack on a fresh GPU box — UCX, nixl, libsirius, StarRocks FE, and the Rust CN. Use when standing the stack up from scratch, recovering a broken toolchain (g++/ld/nvml shims, CUDA 13, no-root conda deps), applying the StarRocks proto patch, or relocating pixi/cargo/Maven onto local NVMe.
- cn-tuning: Size Sirius StarRocks CN memory and operator budgets for a given GPU box and TPC-H scale factor. Use when choosing GPU_MEM, STAGING, HOST_MEM, hash_partition_bytes, scan_task_batch_size, or when a query OOMs / exhausts the exchange arena / looks like an engine bug that is actually mis-sizing. Covers the derived-flag path vs a full sirius.yaml.
- dataset-manager: Use this skill to generate benchmark datasets (TPC-H, TPC-DS, etc.). Trigger when the user needs test data at a specific scale factor for benchmarking or testing. Supports parquet and duckdb output formats.
- log-analyzer: Use this skill to analyze Sirius query execution logs — to find why a query is slow, diagnose validation errors (wrong results), spot excessive downgrading, identify pipeline gaps, or compare two runs of the same query. Trigger whenever the user mentions a Sirius log file, says "look at this log", asks about per-operator time, pipeline gaps, memory pressure, downgrade behavior, validation/correctness mismatches, or wants to compare two query runs. Also use as a hand-off target from race-check (for two-run comparisons), runtime-errors (for "where did the query stall before hang"), and validate (for diffing the bad run against a good run). This is the log-only counterpart to profile-analyzer (nsys) and optimization-advisor (source-level guidance).
- module-context: Automatically identify which dependency library modules are relevant to a task and load their API documentation into context. Use PROACTIVELY before implementing features, fixing bugs, or writing new operators — analyzes the task description and loads cudf, rmm, duckdb, cucascade module docs to improve code quality. Trigger when the user asks to implement, add, fix, or modify GPU operators, pipeline components, memory management, joins, aggregations, sorting, expressions, or data I/O.
- module-discover: Discover and document a dependency library or submodule — analyzes all uses within the codebase, divides the library into logical modules, identifies which modules are used, and generates LLM-consumable API documentation for each module. Use when the user wants to understand a library dependency, map its modules, or generate API reference docs for a submodule.
- optimization-advisor: Use this skill to find exactly which source code to optimize for better GPU performance. Maps nsys profile hotspots to specific Sirius source files and functions, classifies bottlenecks as GPU-bound, CPU-bound, or sync-bound, and recommends actionable code changes. Trigger when the user wants to know what to optimize, where to focus coding effort, or wants source-level optimization guidance. This skill focuses on actionable source code targets — for generating performance reports and measurements, use profile-analyzer instead.
- pr-digest: Generates a "learning" PR-review digest — a markdown file at PR_digests/PR_digest_<N>.md that explains what a GitHub PR does, why, and exactly where in the code, with clickable file/line links and trimmed diffs. Use this whenever the user shares a GitHub PR URL (e.g. github.com/owner/repo/pull/1234) and wants to understand, summarize, review, walk through, or get up to speed on what changed — phrases like "can you review this PR", "what does this PR do", "help me understand this pull request", "summarize the changes in PR
- pre-commit-cleanup: Clean the current Git changes before committing. Use when preparing to commit or when the pre-commit cleanliness hook blocks a commit.
- profile-analyzer: Use this skill to understand why a Sirius query is slow, identify GPU bottlenecks, or detect performance regressions. Generates reports with kernel occupancy, memory bandwidth, operator attribution, and cross-run comparisons. Trigger when the user mentions profiling, nsys, GPU utilization, kernel analysis, performance reports, or wants to compare query timings across runs. This skill focuses on measurement and reporting — for mapping hotspots to source code fixes, use optimization-advisor instead.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- tpch-2host: Bring up Sirius StarRocks CNs across two physical GB200 hosts with nixl over cross-host NVLink, and the matching stock StarRocks (engine B) two-machine baseline. Use when replicating the two-host experiment, setting SIRIUS_EXCHANGE_STAGING_ARENA=fabric, debugging a 0.4 GB/s cuda_ipc fallback, or running engine B as 1 FE + 1 BE per host.
- tpch-bench: Operate the Sirius-as-StarRocks-CN demo and its TPC-H benchmark on the 4x GB200 box. Use when bringing the multi-GPU (N-CN, one CN per GPU) cluster up or down, running a query or the 22-query sweep, verifying the nixl/NVLink transport, triaging a failing/hanging/slow query, checking results against DuckDB, or reproducing the A-vs-B comparison against stock StarRocks.
- tpch-cn-sweep: Run the 22-query TPC-H sweep against a Sirius StarRocks CN cluster on any box, scale factor, data path, or GPU count. Use when launching bench.sh, sizing GPU_MEM/STAGING, checking results against the DuckDB oracle, or triaging pass/wedge/refused rows. Not the in-process Sirius-vs-DuckDB benchmark skill; not the GB200-hardcoded tpch-bench ops skill.
- update-docs: Use this skill to update Super Sirius documentation after code changes. Trigger when the user says "update docs", "refresh documentation", "sync docs with code changes", or after merging PRs that changed the Super Sirius codebase. Inspects merged PRs since the last update and patches affected doc files.

- anthropic-skills:learn: Use this skill when the user wants intellectual understanding — learning how or why something works, not getting a task done or soliciting Claude's judgment.

Trigger for:
- Explicit learning requests: teach, explain, ELI5, walk me through, quiz me, flashcards, "I'm rusty on"; definitions ("what is X")
- Terse concept names implying "help me understand this": "Galois theory," "transformers, from scratch"
- Confusion signals: "won't stick," "keep mixing these up," "not getting it"
- Learning-path questions: prerequisites, sequencing, what to study before X
- Conceptual questions about mechanisms, causes, or dynamics

- Tasks: coding, writing, calculation, translation, factual lookup, news updates
- Personal troubleshooting; resource/textbook recommendations

Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

22	1. FE StatisticsCalculator.computeFileScanNode sets outputRowCount = 1 for FILES() scans ("we don't know the real schema in file, just use the default Row Count now"); every column statistic UNKNOWN. 24	3. Engine OOM handling: gpu_pipeline_executor.cpp reschedules a task on OOM up to MAX_RETRIES=100 with a 50 ms sleep, then fails the query ("exceeded maximum retry limit"). 39	   1-CN q04: scan fragment 37 tasks, Queued sum 19.9 s vs Computing 4.7 s inside a 1.2 s wall; join fragment requested 253 GB of reservations for a 61 GB summed peak (4x over-estimate).

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Per-query, per-pipeline, per-operator summary of one Quent session dir (ndjson exporter).
usage: quent_summary.py <session_dir> [label]"""
import json, sys, glob, collections
s = sys.argv[1]; label = sys.argv[2] if len(sys.argv) > 2 else s
def rows(kind):
    for f in glob.glob(f"{s}/{kind}/*.ndjson"):
        for l in open(f):
            j = json.loads(l); st = j["data"].get("state", j["data"]); k = st if isinstance(st, str) else next(iter(st))
            yield j["id"], j["timestamp"], k, (st if isinstance(st, dict) else {})
# queries
q = collections.defaultdict(dict)
for qid, ts, k, st in rows("query"):
    q[qid].setdefault("t0", ts); q[qid]["t1"] = ts
    if k == "Init": q[qid]["name"] = st["Init"].get("instance_name")
    if k == "Executing": q[qid]["exec"] = ts
# pipelines (operator Declaration) -> query via plan
plan_q = {}
for pid, ts, k, st in rows("plan"):
    plan_q[pid] = st.get("Declaration", {}).get("parent", {}).get("query_id")
pipe = {}
for oid, ts, k, st in rows("operator"):
    d = st.get("Declaration", {}); pipe[oid] = (plan_q.get(d.get("plan_id")), d.get("instance_name"), d.get("type_name"))
# tasks
tasks = collections.defaultdict(list)
for tid, ts, k, st in rows("task"): tasks[tid].append((ts, k, st))
agg = collections.defaultdict(lambda: collections.defaultdict(lambda: [0, 0.0, 0]))  # (qid,pipe) -> op -> [n, secs, bytes]
pipe_tasks = collections.Counter(); queue_wait = collections.defaultdict(float); span = {}
for tid, ev in tasks.items():
    ev.sort(); pu = next((st["Created"]["pipeline_uuid"] for _, k, st in ev if k == "Created"), None)
    if pu is None: continue
    qid = pipe.get(pu, (None,))[0]; key = (qid, pu); pipe_tasks[key] += 1
    for i, (ts, k, st) in enumerate(ev):
        nxt = ev[i + 1][0] if i + 1 < len(ev) else ts
        if k == "Computing":
            c = st["Computing"]; a = agg[key][c.get("instance_name")]; a[0] += 1; a[1] += (nxt - ts) / 1e9; a[2] += c.get("input_bytes") or 0
        elif k in ("Queued",): queue_wait[key] += (nxt - ts) / 1e9
        elif k in ("Reserving", "Preparing", "Routing", "Finalizing"): agg[key]["_" + k][1] += (nxt - ts) / 1e9
    t0 = ev[0][0]; t1 = ev[-1][0]; sp = span.setdefault(key, [t0, t1]); sp[0] = min(sp[0], t0); sp[1] = max(sp[1], t1)
# data batches per producer pipeline
batches = collections.defaultdict(lambda: [0, 0])
for bid, ts, k, st in rows("data_batch"):
    if k == "Constructed": batches[st["Constructed"]["producer_pipeline_uuid"]][0] += 1
    if k == "Stationary":
        m = st["Stationary"].get("memory", {}).get("capacity", {}) or {}; 
print(f"##### {label}")
for qid, info in sorted(q.items(), key=lambda x: x[1]["t0"]):
    wall = (info["t1"] - info["t0"]) / 1e9
    print(f"query {qid[-12:]} {info.get('name')} wall={wall:.3f}s")
    for (qq, pu), ops in agg.items():
        if qq != qid: continue
        name = pipe[pu][1]; sp = span[(qq, pu)]
        print(f"  pipeline {pipe[pu][2]} [{name}] tasks={pipe_tasks[(qq,pu)]} span={(sp[1]-sp[0])/1e9:.3f}s queue_wait_sum={queue_wait[(qq,pu)]:.3f}s batches_out={batches[pu][0]}")
        for op, (n, secs, b) in sorted(ops.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1][1]):
            if op.startswith("_"): print(f"      {op[1:]:<16} sum={secs:8.3f}s"); continue
            print(f"      {op:<20} n={n:4d} sum={secs:8.3f}s avg={secs/max(n,1)*1000:8.1f}ms input_GB={b/1e9:7.2f}")

## 1. Timings (results.md, warm medians, ms)

| q | standalone | 1 CN | 4 CN | 1CN/standalone | 1CN/4CN |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| q03 | 3050 | 3106 | 1607 | 1.02 | 1.93 |

OOM reschedules: 0 in every run of these queries on both CN arms (cn1-cnlog.txt, cn4-cnlog.txt).

## 2. FE plan vs actual rows per exchange

1 CN (survey/plan-summary.txt, card-compare-cn1.txt): every join BROADCAST, every cardinality 1.
- q03: 9:INNER JOIN (BROADCAST) build=exch8<-orders(x customer) 145,769,513 rows; 6: build=exch5<-customer 29,998,152
- q10: 13: build=exch12<-lineitem(x orders) 114,711,320; 10: build=exch9<-orders 57,358,391; 3: build=exch2<-nation 25
- q12: 4: build=exch3<-lineitem 31,162,904 (probe orders 1.5B)
- q14: 4: build=exch3<-part 200,000,000 (probe lineitem-filtered ~75M)
- q19: 4: build=exch3<-lineitem 128,557,109 (probe part; part filter applied inside the fragment: 2.16M rows)

4 CN (survey/plan-summary-4cn.txt, card-compare-cn4.txt): the big joins flip to PARTITIONED (shuffle both sides):
- q03: exch2 SHUFFLE lineitem 3,234,397,656 rows; exch9 SHUFFLE orders 145,769,513; exch6 BROADCAST customer 119,992,608 (=30M x 4)
- q10: exch8 SHUFFLE lineitem 1,480,675,200; exch5 SHUFFLE customer 150,000,000; exch11 orders 57M; exch14 114.7M; nation BROADCAST
- q12: exch1 SHUFFLE orders 1,500,000,000; exch4 lineitem 31,162,904
- q14: exch4 SHUFFLE part 200,000,000; exch2 lineitem 74,818,904
- q19: exch4 SHUFFLE lineitem 128,557,109; exch1 part 2,158,428

Why it flips (FE source): StatisticsCalculator.computeFileScanNode (fe-core .../statistics/StatisticsCalculator.java:664-676) sets outputRowCount=1 and every column UNKNOWN;
Statistics.getOutputSize (Statistics.java:88-108) = sum(type widths) x 1; CostModel.visitPhysicalDistribution (cost/CostModel.java:401-432):
BROADCAST cost = outputSize x aliveBackendNumber, SHUFFLE cost = outputSize (x factor). So with N=1 broadcast beats shuffling both sides; with N=4 shuffle wins unless the build side is narrow
(customer c_custkey 4B vs orders 16B -> customer stays BROADCAST). EnforceAndCostTask.checkBroadcastRowCountLimit (task/EnforceAndCostTask.java:281-322) never trips: rowCount 1 <= broadcastRowCountLimit 15,000,000.
=> The distribution choice is a function of column type widths and alive-node count only.

Bytes actually moved at 4 CN (cn4-transmits.txt; per-stream from cluster.log 'transmitted batches via nixl'):
| q | nixl total GB | dominant stream | alternative (1-CN plan generalised: broadcast small side, big table local) |
|---|---|---|---|
| q03 | 60.34 | lineitem 4x14.5 = 58 GB (3x4.85 GB frames per CN) | broadcast orders x customer 2.33 GB parked -> 3x2.33 = 7 GB |
| q10 | 48.04 | lineitem 26.6 GB + customer 19.2 GB | broadcast orders-filtered 0.70 GB (2.1 GB) + lineitem x orders 2.29 GB (6.9 GB) = 9 GB |
| q12 | 23.47 | orders 4x5.8 = 23.2 GB | broadcast lineitem-filtered 0.51 GB -> 1.5 GB |
| q14 | 5.43 | part 4.3 GB + lineitem 1.1 GB | broadcast lineitem-filtered 1.52 GB -> 4.6 GB (wash) |
| q19 | 2.75 | lineitem-filtered 2.75 GB | broadcast part-filtered 0.02 GB -> 0.06 GB |
(parked sizes at 1 CN: cn1-ops.txt STREAMING_SOURCE/SINK input_GB: q03 a208 2.33, q10 315e sink 0.70 / 315d sink 2.29, q12 69b sink 0.51, q14 c4 sink 5.77 / c3 PARTITION(4) 1.52, q19 96d sink 3.66, 96c CONCAT(3) 0.02)

## 3. What DuckDB standalone chose (standalone/runs/qNN.explain.txt)

- q03: HASH_JOIN build = (orders x customer) est 61.6M, probe lineitem est 1.22B -- same shape as the FE 1-CN plan.
- q10: build = (lineitem x orders) est 244M, probe customer x nation est 151.5M -- same as FE 1-CN.
- q12: build = lineitem-filtered est 244M, probe orders est 1.54B -- same.
- q14: build = part est 203M, probe lineitem est 1.22B (actual 75M!) -- same as FE; both wrong vs actual (lineitem-filtered 75M < part 200M).
- q19: build = part-filtered est 8.1M (derived filters pushed), probe lineitem est 1.22B -- OPPOSITE to FE (FE build = lineitem exchange 128.5M).
DuckDB's parquet estimates: lineitem 1.22B (actual 6B), orders 308M (actual 1.5B), customer 151.5M, part 203M.

## 4. Engine-side re-planning inside the receiver fragment (fact 11 mechanism)

engine.rs:540-585 declares the exact parked row count per stream before build(); stream_bind_catalog.hpp:44-46 feeds it to DuckDB's TableFunction cardinality callback.
DuckDB join-order (query_graph_manager.cpp:264-266): right child = build = smaller estimated cardinality. DuckDB JoinFilterPushdown pushes build-side filters into PROBE-side scans
(join_filter_pushdown_optimizer.cpp:61-134); Sirius wraps the probe leaf (GPU_SCAN or STREAMING_SOURCE) in DYNAMIC_FILTER (sirius_physical_plan_generator.cpp:296-324).
=> DYNAMIC_FILTER on X means X is a probe side.

Translated plans (cn1/cluster.log 'translated StarRocks plan fragment' blocks, lines ~3184 q03, 12533 q10, 14162 q12, 15297 q14, 18958 q19):
- q19 receiver 996c: Join(Filter[p_size<=15 ...](part Read), sirius_stream_3). cn1-ops.txt 6493-6546: STREAMING_SOURCE(4)->DYNAMIC_FILTER(5) 120 tasks 3.66GB -> 0.01GB; HASH_JOIN(9) n=1 in=0.02GB. => build = part (est 203M x 0.2 x 0.2 ~ 8.1M; actual 2.16M), probe = lineitem stream. Engine flipped the FE's build side. Fragment 150 ms.
- q10 receiver 315c: Join(Project(Join(Filter[is_not_null($0)](customer Read), stream_2 nation)), stream_12). cn1-ops.txt 3437-3573: Pipeline 9 [STREAMING_SOURCE(10)->DYNAMIC_FILTER(11)] 17 tasks 2.29GB => the 114.7M-row stream is PROBE; build = customer x nation (150M rows, PARTITION(8) 25.55GB 0.479s, CONCAT(9) 0.114s, HASH_JOIN(14) 0.301s).
  Cause: DuckDB RelationStatisticsHelper::DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY = 0.2 (duckdb/src/include/duckdb/optimizer/join_order/relation_statistics_helper.hpp:57, applied .cpp:149) on the FE's null-rejecting scan conjunct (translated by expr_translator.rs:630/929 'is_not_null_pred'): customer 150M x 0.2 = 30M < 114.7M declared. Standalone (no is_not_null) estimates customer x nation 151.5M and has no DYNAMIC_FILTER on the lineitem x orders side.
- q12 receiver 69a: Filter[is_not_null](orders Read) est 1.54B x 0.2 = 308M vs stream 31.2M -> build = stream (sensible). q14 c3: lineitem Read (date filter) 1.22B x 0.2 = 244M vs stream part 200M -> build = part (same as standalone; actual lineitem 75M would be better). q03 a208: lineitem 1.22B x 0.2 = 244M vs stream 145.8M -> build = stream.

findings.claim: The FE's BROADCAST-vs-SHUFFLE decision is data-blind: with FILES() scans fixed at cardinality 1, the cost model reduces to (column type widths x alive-node count), so at 1 CN every join is BROADCAST (harmless, single destination) and at 4 CN the big joins flip to PARTITIONED and shuffle the LARGE table instead of broadcasting the small side. For q03/q10/q12/q19 this moves 5-45x more bytes across GPUs than the natural plan (the 1-CN shape generalised).
evidence: FE mechanism (measured in source): StatisticsCalculator.java:664-676 computeFileScanNode sets outputRowCount=1, all columns UNKNOWN; Statistics.java:88-108 getOutputSize = sum(type widths) x 1; CostModel.java:401-432 BROADCAST cost = outputSize x aliveBackendNumber, SHUFFLE = outputSize; EnforceAndCostTask.java:281-322 checkBroadcastRowCountLimit never fires (rowCount 1 <= 15,000,000).

survey/plan-summary.txt vs plan-summary-4cn.txt: q03 9:INNER JOIN BROADCAST build=orders -> 10:INNER JOIN (PARTITIONED) build=exch9<-orders probe=exch2<-lineitem; q10 13: BROADCAST build=lineitem -> 12:/15: PARTITIONED; q12/q14/q19 4: BROADCAST -> 5: PARTITIONED. Narrow build sides stay BROADCAST at 4 CN (q03 customer 4 B/row, q10 nation), matching the width-only cost.

card-compare-cn4.txt actual rows shuffled: q03 exch2 lineitem 3,234,397,656 + exch9 orders 145,769,513; q10 exch8 lineitem 1,480,675,200 + exch5 customer 150,000,000; q12 exch1 orders 1,500,000,000 (to meet 31,162,904 lineitem rows); q19 exch4 lineitem 128,557,109 (to meet 2,158,428 part rows).
cn4-transmits.txt bytes over nixl per query: q03 60.34 GB (58 GB is lineitem: 3 frames x 4.82-4.89 GB per CN), q10 48.04 GB (lineitem 26.6 + customer 19.2), q12 23.47 GB, q19 2.75 GB, q14 5.43 GB.

Size of the small side that could be broadcast instead (parked bytes at 1 CN, cn1-ops.txt STREAMING_SINK/SOURCE input_GB): q03 orders x customer 2.33 GB (=> 3x2.33 = 7 GB traffic vs 60 GB); q10 orders-filtered 0.70 GB + lineitem x orders 2.29 GB (=> 9 GB vs 48 GB); q12 lineitem-filtered 0.51 GB (=> 1.5 GB vs 23.5 GB); q19 part-filtered 0.02 GB (=> 0.06 GB vs 2.75 GB); q14 lineitem-filtered 1.52 GB (=> 4.6 GB vs 5.4 GB, a wash).

standalone/runs/q03,q10,q12.explain.txt: DuckDB (with parquet stats) builds on the same small sides the 1-CN FE plan broadcasts (orders x customer est 61.6M; lineitem x orders est 244M; lineitem-filtered est 244M).
Measured wall cost of the shuffle at 4 CN (see BJ-2/BJ-3): q03 0.28 s/CN drain + 0.5 s arena dwell out of a 1.42 s span; 4-CN speed-up 1.93-2.14x (results-ratios.md).
findings.impact: At 4 CN, 15-25% of q03/q10/q12 wall time is spent moving and staging the large table (drains alone: q03 0.28 s of 1.42 s, q10 0.24 s of 1.47 s, q12 0.12 s of 1.07 s) and the receive arena holds up to 88% of its capacity (BJ-3); at 1 CN the decision costs nothing. The FE's fragment cut is fixed before the engine sees any real cardinality, so neither the receiver-first exact-cardinality mechanism nor the translator can undo it (fact 11; node_translator.rs:1924-1931).
findings.proposed_change: Give computeFileScanNode a real outputRowCount for FILES() tables: cheapest is bytes-based (TableFunctionTable.fileStatuses already carries TBrokerFileStatus sizes: rows ~= sum(size)/estimated row width); exact is to return parquet num_rows from the CN's get_file_schema RPC (file_schema.rs already opens the footer). Even a row-count-only estimate re-arms checkBroadcastRowCountLimit (15M) and makes BROADCAST vs SHUFFLE cost proportional to actual sizes, so q03/q10/q12/q19 would broadcast the filtered small side and keep lineitem/orders local at 4 CN. Confidence high on mechanism; medium (inferred) that the wall gain is ~0.2-0.4 s per query at 4 CN, larger at higher SF (BJ-3).

findings.claim: On the CN the shuffle drain is fully serialised: each sender fragment's remote outputs are packed and written one destination at a time AFTER the fragment finishes, on a single transport thread, and the dispatch worker joins those drains before it starts the next queued fragment. 92% of each per-destination transmit is the pack (export_packed_next on the engine thread), not the nixl write.
evidence: cn4/cluster.log q03.r1 (lines 10260-11250; agent-notes section 6): lineitem senders finished at 609-683 ms; sender ec5f's three transmits (4.82-4.89 GB each) completed +95/+190/+283 ms after finish; every transmit line reads elapsed_ms=93-96 lease_ms=1 write_ms=6-8 write_gbps=597-717; the next fragment on that CN (customer scan) started at +0.283-0.287 s after finish on all 4 CNs (computed table in agent-notes: finished->last transmit == next-fragment start).

Same pattern q10.r1: lineitem senders drain 0.145-0.159 s (3 x 2.2 GB), customer senders 0.083-0.102 s, next fragment starts exactly after; q12.r1 orders senders 0.115-0.125 s; q19 0.055-0.078 s; q14 0.02-0.03 s.

All 16 fragment RPCs of q03 arrived within 44.708-44.719 (exec_plan_fragment lines), yet the independent customer scan ran only at +0.89-0.97 s and orders x customer at +1.01 s: critical path = 0.68 lineitem scan + 0.28 drain + 0.04 customer + 0.28 orders x customer + 0.13 join + gaps = 1.42 s span.

Source: compute_node_service.rs:1207-1219 comment: 'one FIFO request channel into ONE transport thread ... the drains still run one at a time, in the FE's destination order'; compute_node_service.rs:376-392 dispatch_worker 'Executes ready receiver fragments sequentially' and run_ready_fragment (:864-872) `.and_then(FragmentOutcome::join_into_ready)` joins the drains inside the call; nixl_transport.rs:713-813 drain loop: `export_packed_next` per batch, then lease RPC, then write_and_wait; engine.rs:813 export_packed_next = engine_call (runs on the engine thread); engine.rs:242-280 one engine thread serving requests serially.
cn4-quent.txt q03.r1: sender fragments show Quent wall 1.28 s vs CN elapsed 0.61-0.68 s (the difference is parked/drain lifetime); leases 117-121 per CN, maxconc 55-56.
findings.impact: For q03 at 4 CN, ~0.3 s of the 1.42 s span is drain (20%), and a further ~0.3 s is small fragments that could have overlapped the lineitem scan; q10 ~0.24 s, q12 ~0.12 s. This is the main reason the scan-heavy queries of this family reach only 1.9-2.1x on 4 CNs (efficiency 0.48-0.53) on top of the per-task scan slowdown (BJ-5). It also amplifies BJ-1: every byte the FE decides to shuffle is paid at ~50 GB/s effective (pack-bound) rather than the 700 GB/s the NVLink write achieves.
findings.proposed_change: (a) Pack for remote destinations during execution (STREAMING_SINK could pack each batch straight into a staging lease, or export_packed_next could run on a dedicated CUDA stream/thread) so the post-finish drain is only the 6-8 ms writes; (b) one transport session/thread per peer so the 3 destinations drain concurrently — per-destination FIFO is all seq/eos/drop_parked ordering needs; (c) in dispatch_worker, start the next queued sender while a drain is in flight (it already dispatches ready receivers first; extend that to queued senders). Expected gain (inferred): 0.15-0.3 s per shuffle stage at 4 CN for q03/q10/q12 (10-20% of wall).

findings.claim: Receiver-first rendezvous plus shuffle-the-big-table means the whole remote portion of a shuffled stream must sit in the receiving CN's staging arena before the receiver runs; q03 at SF1000 already fills 88% of the 16 GiB arena for ~0.5 s, and arena exhaustion is a hard query failure, not backpressure.
evidence: cn4/cluster.log q03.r1 receiver ec53 (9102) 'received remote batches': stream 2 4,888,500,480 + 4,842,342,336 + 4,850,550,720 bytes; stream 9 3 x ~146 MB; stream 6 3 x ~30 MB => 15.1 GB = 14.1 GiB of 16 GiB (capture-cn.sh: SIRIUS_EXCHANGE_STAGING_BYTES=16GiB). Same on the other 3 CNs (14.5-14.7 GB of stream 2 each).

Dwell: frames land 13:19:45.42-45.62 ('transmitted batches via nixl'), consumed 46.014-46.030 ('received remote batches') => 0.4-0.6 s in the arena while customer and orders x customer fragments run in between (receiver cannot start until all 4 senders are complete: local_exchange.rs take_ready :248-267; engine.rs:540-585 needs every contributor's row count before build()).
cn4-quent.txt q03.r1: leases=474 / 122.67 GB / lease_held 105 s summed, max 55-56 concurrent per CN; q10.r1 660 leases, maxconc 62-74; q12.r1 496 leases.

Exhaustion path (source): exchange_staging_arena.cpp:245-258 throws invalid_input_exception 'exchange staging arena exhausted ... (raise SIRIUS_EXCHANGE_STAGING_BYTES)'; nixl_transport.rs:720 `rpc_request_lease(...)?` propagates the error out of the drain; no wait or retry (only warmup.rs has backoff, for peer discovery).

At 1 CN nothing is staged (0 leases in cn1-quent.txt); the parked intermediate lives as long as a hash table would in standalone (q03 2.33 GB parked 0.5 s; q19 3.66 GB parked ~2.6 s while the lineitem fragment runs).
findings.impact: Scaling cliff rather than a slowdown: with the current FE plan the arena requirement for q03 grows with lineitem/N (14.6 GB per CN at SF1000), so ~SF1150 with STAGING=16GiB, or SF1000 with a 12 GiB arena, fails q03 outright after all the scan work is done. The same plan shape (BJ-1) puts q10 at 6.7+4.8 GB and q12 at 5.8 GB per CN. Broadcasting the small side instead would need <1 GB of arena per CN for every query in this family.
findings.proposed_change: Short term: fix BJ-1 (broadcast the small side) and document that STAGING must cover the largest shuffled stream / N. Engine side: make exchange_staging_arena::lease block (bounded, with a condition variable on release) instead of throwing, so a full arena applies backpressure to senders rather than failing the query; or let the receiver push remote frames into pool memory on arrival (push_packed is already a deep copy into the pool) and release the lease immediately, keeping only the per-frame row count for declare_input_cardinality. Confidence high on the measured occupancy and failure path; medium on the SF extrapolation.

findings.claim: Inside a fragment the receiver-first exact stream cardinality works and lets the engine override the FE's build side when the FE is wrong (q19), but the OTHER side of the join is estimated by DuckDB's join-order heuristics without statistics, and the FE's null-rejecting `IS NOT NULL` scan conjunct (translated to a Filter rel) costs a flat 0.2 selectivity, which in q10 flips the build to the 150M-row, 25.5 GB customer side instead of the 114.7M-row, 2.3 GB stream.
evidence: q19 1-CN: FE plan build=3:EXCHANGE<-lineitem (128,557,109 rows) probe=part (survey/plan-summary.txt); engine receiver 996c (cn1-ops.txt 6493-6546): Pipeline 3 [STREAMING_SOURCE(4)->DYNAMIC_FILTER(5)] 120 tasks 3.66 GB -> 0.01 GB, HASH_JOIN(9) n=1 in=0.02 GB, fragment 150 ms => the lineitem stream is the probe, part-filtered (DuckDB est 203M x 0.2 x 0.2 ~ 8.1M, actual 2.16M) is the build. Same shape as standalone (q19.explain.txt build = part est 8,134,748).

Mechanism: engine.rs:540-585 declares exact rows; stream_bind_catalog.hpp:44-46 feeds the TableFunction cardinality callback; DuckDB query_graph_manager.cpp:264-266 puts the smaller estimate on the right (build); join_filter_pushdown_optimizer.cpp:61-134 pushes build-side filters into probe-side scans and sirius_physical_plan_generator.cpp:296-324 wraps that probe leaf in DYNAMIC_FILTER — so DYNAMIC_FILTER on X marks X as probe.

q10 1-CN receiver 315c translated plan (cn1/cluster.log ~line 12533): Join(Project(Join(Filter[is_not_null($0)](customer Read), sirius_stream_2)), sirius_stream_12); cn1-ops.txt 3437-3573: Pipeline 9 [STREAMING_SOURCE(10)->DYNAMIC_FILTER(11)] 17 tasks 2.29 GB => the stream (114,711,320 declared rows) is the probe; the build is customer x nation: PARTITION(8) 25.55 GB 0.479 s, CONCAT(9) 0.114 s, HASH_JOIN(14) 0.301 s on 27.7 GB.

DuckDB RelationStatisticsHelper::DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY = 0.2 (duckdb/src/include/duckdb/optimizer/join_order/relation_statistics_helper.hpp:57; applied relation_statistics_helper.cpp:149, relation_manager.cpp:199-374) => customer 150M x 0.2 = 30M < 114.7M. The is_not_null comes from an FE scan conjunct translated by expr_translator.rs:630/929 ('is_not_null_pred' -> Substrait is_not_null); it is absent from q03/q14/q19 translated plans and from the standalone plan, whose customer x nation estimate is 151,574,782 and which has no DYNAMIC_FILTER on the lineitem x orders side (standalone-ops.txt 2420-2533).

q12 receiver has the same Filter[is_not_null] on orders (1.54B x 0.2 = 308M vs stream 31.2M) so the build side stays correct there; q14 engine builds on part (200M) rather than the 75M-row filtered lineitem stream in both CN and standalone because DuckDB's lineitem estimate is 1.22B x 0.2 = 244M (HASH_JOIN(6) only 0.113 s, so harmless).
findings.impact: For this family the mis-pick costs little wall time at SF1000 (q10 receiver fragment 1.07 s vs ~0.8 s equivalent in standalone; q10 is the only query of the family with a 1-CN/standalone ratio above 1.13), but the hash-table side is 11x larger in bytes than needed (25.5 GB vs 2.3 GB), which is the quantity that must be GPU-resident and that grows with SF and with the wide-payload joins of q07/q08/q09. The exact-cardinality mechanism itself adds no cost (the intermediate is parked anyway).
findings.proposed_change: In the translator, do not emit the FE's null-rejecting `col IS NOT NULL` join-key conjunct as a Filter rel when the column is a join key (the join drops nulls anyway; the FE emits it for its own BE), or attach it to the ReadRel as a table filter so DuckDB's estimator does not apply DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY to it; alternatively teach the FFI planner's relation statistics to treat IS NOT NULL as selectivity 1.0. Verify with the q10 receiver's Substrait from cn1/dump (plan-*.substrait) through the FFI planner and confirm the DYNAMIC_FILTER moves to the customer scan. Confidence medium: the DYNAMIC_FILTER placement is measured; the 0.2-selectivity arithmetic is inferred from DuckDB source, not from a printed estimate.

findings.claim: Per-task GPU_SCAN Computing time rises 1.3-1.6x when four CNs scan the same dataset concurrently on one host, which by itself caps the 4-CN speed-up of these scan-dominated queries at ~2.5-3x before any exchange cost; measured 1.9-2.1x.
evidence: Per-task GPU_SCAN Computing on the big scans (cn1-quent.json / cn4-quent.json / standalone-quent.json top_ops; ms per ~2.2-2.3 GB task): q03 lineitem 102 (1 CN) vs 134-145 (4 CN) vs 111 (standalone); q10 lineitem 90 vs 100-119 vs 96; q12 orders 107 vs 131-146 vs 117; q14 lineitem 151 vs 240-249 vs 176; q19 lineitem 85 vs 113-126 vs 98.

Fragment walls follow: q03 lineitem sender 609-683 ms for 36.4-36.8 GB per CN (53-60 GB/s) vs 2193 ms for 146 GB at 1 CN (67 GB/s); q14 lineitem 904-920 ms per CN at 4 CN for 30.5 GB (33 GB/s) vs 2330 ms for 122 GB at 1 CN (52 GB/s).

results-ratios.md: 4-CN speed-up q03 1.93, q10 2.07, q12 1.96, q14 2.11, q19 2.14 (efficiency 0.48-0.53); the scan is 75-95% of each 1-CN query (cn1-quent.txt Computing sums: q19 GPU_SCAN 10.16 of 10.8 s, q14 8.46 of 8.9 s).
scan_split_read probe recorded counts only (bytes=0, ns=0 for every fragment in cn*-quent.json), so file-read time cannot be separated from decode.
findings.impact: Together with BJ-2 this explains the whole gap between the ideal 4x and the measured ~2x for q03/q12/q14/q19: roughly half the loss is per-CN scan throughput under contention, half is serialisation on the CN. It is not specific to broadcast joins but is the dominant limiter for this family at 4 CN.
findings.proposed_change: Instrument scan_split_read with bytes and elapsed_ns (the probe exists but records neither), then A/B a pure-scan query (q06 or q14) at 1 vs 4 CN with the page cache warm vs dropped to attribute the slowdown to NVMe/page-cache read bandwidth vs host->GPU staging vs decode. Cause is inferred (shared host I/O or C2C bandwidth on one GB200 host); only the per-task slowdown is measured.

findings.claim: Memory backpressure is absent for this family at both 1 and 4 CN: zero OOM reschedules, Reserving waits under 0.2 s per query, no arena exhaustion; the 6-15x reservation over-estimate is harmless here because the 4-slot executor keeps concurrent reservations far below the 100 GiB pool, and the large Queued sums are slot queueing.
evidence: cn1-cnlog.txt / cn4-cnlog.txt: oom_resched=0 for every run of q03 q10 q12 q14 q19 on both arms; engine-log warnings in the 13:19-13:29 window are unrelated (slot_for_device fallback, no-scan fragments).

reservation-ratio.txt cn1: q03 req 698.8 GB vs peak 49.3 GB (14.2x), q14 381.6 vs 25.1 (15.2x), q10 6.3x, q12 1.8x, q19 1.2x; standalone q14 68x. Yet Reserving state sums (cn1-quent.txt r1): q10 0.180 s, q14 0.138 s, q12 0.110 s, q03 0.003 s, q19 0.004 s; cn4 fragments <= 0.007 s.

Queued sums (reservation-ratio.txt): cn1 q03 109.9 s, q14 109.7 s, q19 156.4 s, q10 99.3 s; standalone q19 346 s — 56-120 scan tasks waiting for one of 4 pipeline slots (docs/super-sirius/configuration.md:91-94), not for memory.

Parked-intermediate dwell at 1 CN equals the build side's natural lifetime (q03 2.33 GB parked 0.5 s during the orders x customer -> lineitem handoff; q19 3.66 GB for ~2.6 s while the lineitem fragment runs), the same as a hash table in standalone; fragment-boundary overhead is relay + CONCAT (q03 CONCAT(2) 13 ms on 2.33 GB).
findings.impact: Negative result that scopes the other findings: for q03/q10/q12/q14/q19 the losses are planning (BJ-1), CN serialisation (BJ-2) and scan contention (BJ-5), not memory pressure; the reservation over-estimate should be pursued with the OOM-failing queries (q05/q08/q09/q17/q18/q21), not here.
findings.proposed_change: None for this family. If the reservation estimator is tuned for the OOM family, re-check q14/q03 (15x, 14x) as regression guards that a tighter estimate does not start gating scan tasks.
